newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China Light may "do something" on Black Pt.
newsitem.headline: China Light may "do something" on Black Pt.

text.p: China Light and Power Co Ltd said on Monday it might be able to "do something" about two of four units at its Black Point power station it is under pressure to delay or cancel because of overcapacity.
Chairman Sidney Gordon told reporters that halting work on units five and six at Black Point power station was not practical.
But the company "might be able to do something" about Black Point's units seven and eight, he said. He did not elaborate.
The outgoing chairman, who will retire and be succeeded by Michael Kadoorie on Tuesday, said China Light was aware it had too much capacity.

"We accept the criticism that we underestimated the speed at which Hong Kong's manufacturing sector would relocate to China in the early part of the 1990s," Gordon earlier told the company's annual general meeting.

Construction of Black Point, the world's largest natural gas fired power plant, began in 1993, but the company has come under pressure to halt or delay commissioning of four of the plant's eight units due to slowing growth in electricity demand.
Black Point consists of eight 312 MW units. Two units were commissioned in mid-1996 and two will be turned on in mid-1997.
The Hong Kong government said last month it had asked the utility to submit in three months a detailed plan for deferral.
The company's earnings growth is tied to the growth in its fixed assets as detailed under a scheme of control worked out between the utility and the government.
The company last month reported group operating earnings of HK$4.84 billion for the year ended September 30, 1996, a 10.2 percent increase before exceptionals over the year earlier.
But unit sales to the manufacturing sector fell by 4.2 percent even though total sales grew by 4.3 percent.

The migration of local industry to China in search of a cheaper production base has resulted in low electricity demand growth, exacerbated by the current normal cyclical contraction of the local economy, company officials said.
"The manufacturing sector, such that remains in the territory, is continuing to feel the brunt of the economic slowdown," said Gordon.
The number of manufacturing establishments in Hong Kong has fallen by one third in six years, he said.

China Light serves Kowloon, the New Territories and outlying islands in Hong Kong. About 20 percent of sales are to industry. The company also sends a limited amount of power to the Shekou Industrial Zone in China under a long-term contract.
The manufacturing sector accounts for less than 3.0 percent of the electricity sales of Hongkong Electric Power Co Ltd, which serves Hong Kong island and Lamma island.

"Management have been engaged in an aggressive programme to reduce both capital and operating expenditures," Gordon said. "We expect tariff increases during the difficult 1997-99 period to be on a par with inflation."
